Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).

I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, fire/flames is a possible but not typical cue unless the disaster specifically involved fire; with the rest of the profile emphasizing silence, people related to the event, intrusive memory, grief, and safety behaviors, this trigger looks trauma-incongruent and insufficiently supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by hypervigilance and strong safety-seeking (e.g., always choosing the safest seat). While mixed patterns can occur, this combination is hard to reconcile here because the other items consistently describe danger avoidance rather than approach to danger.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes lacks coherence with the rest of the profile and with natural-disaster trauma unless clothing was a highly specific trauma cue. No other trigger, memory, or threat item supports a clothes-based association, so this maladaptive strategy appears disconnected from the formulation and selected symptoms.

vignette:
Linh was fifty-two years old, a Vietnamese-American librarian at a public library in a small coastal town, when Hurricane Nadia made landfall three years ago. She and her husband, Sopheap, had decided to ride out the storm at home, a decision she would later replay hundreds of times. The storm surge came fast, pushing water through the ground floor while they climbed to the attic. For hours they listened to the wind scream and the house groan, and then—suddenly, impossibly—silence. The eye. That stillness, the absence of any sound, was the most terrifying moment of her life. She knew the storm would return, and when it did, the noise was even worse, but it was the silence that stayed with her. In the aftermath, they were rescued by neighbours from two houses down, the Parkers, who had a boat. Linh never saw the bodies of the two people who drowned on her street, but she could not stop imagining it. And every time she saw Mr. Parker in the grocery store or Mrs. Parker at the post office, her chest tightened and she felt the same helpless numbness she had felt in the attic. She started crossing the street to avoid them, even though they had saved her life. She told herself it was because she didn’t want to talk about the storm, but the truth was that their faces yanked her straight back into that moment—the cold water, the splintering wood, the awful silence.

In the weeks that followed, Linh tried to return to her normal routines, but the world felt different. She found herself watching the edges of every room, scanning the corners of the stacks at the library, making sure no one was too close. She began choosing her seat in the staff break room with her back to the wall, and at home she insisted on sitting in the chair that faced the front door. Sopheap asked her about it once; she said she just felt safer that way. She did not tell him that she was constantly alert, that her heart jumped every time the silence of a reading room settled around her. At work, she would sometimes find herself holding her breath, listening for something she could not name. One afternoon a patron who resembled Mrs. Parker—same grey hair, same way of standing—approached the reference desk, and Linh felt her vision narrow. She excused herself and went to the staff room, shaking. She could not explain why. She only knew she had to get away.

Nighttime became difficult. Linh began leaving a lamp on in the bedroom, and she woke several times a night, disoriented and afraid, convinced the dark was pressing in. She avoided walking outside after sunset. More troubling, she started to lose attention during conversations. When a patron or a colleague spoke, she would feel herself pulling away, deliberately trying to leave her body, to blank out the moment. It worked, briefly, but then she would come back feeling hollow. She stopped going to the small gym near her home because the exertion made her heart pound and she could not calm down afterward. She told Sopheap she was just tired from work.

But the worst moments came without warning. She could be shelving books in a quiet aisle—the library was always quiet, that was the problem—and suddenly she would be back in the attic, the smell of wet wood in her nostrils, her throat tight. The memory forced its way into her mind, and along with it came an overwhelming wave of grief, so heavy she had to lean against the shelves. She was not just remembering the hurricane; she was mourning the woman she had been before, the one who walked into the dark without a second thought. She began to avoid certain sections of the library—disaster preparedness, weather, anything related to water—and she asked a colleague to cover the evening shifts. She said she needed to be home earlier. She did not explain that being in the dark, even on her own street, made her feel like she was drowning again. The Parkers called once, to check on her, and she let the call go to voicemail. She never called them back. She could not bear to hear their voices, because their voices reminded her of the boat ride through the flooded street, the wreckage, the uncertainty of who had survived.

The consequences accumulated. Her supervisor noted she seemed distracted, and a patron complained that Linh had given a curt answer when asked about a book on hurricanes. Linh withdrew from the small circle of friends she and Sopheap had maintained. She stopped attending the book club she had led for years, claiming scheduling conflicts. In truth, she could not bear the silences that fell between sentences, the way a pause in conversation could send her back to that moment of absolute stillness. She felt trapped between two worlds: the one she lived in, where her body was present, and the one she kept revisiting, where she was powerless.

Linh came to therapy because Sopheap had begged her. He found her one morning standing in the kitchen at three a.m., staring at the wall, having dissociated for so long she did not remember walking there. She agreed to come because she was terrified that she was losing her mind, and more afraid that she would lose her marriage. In the first session, she sat in the chair closest to the door, her back to the wall, her eyes scanning the room twice before she spoke. She said she wanted to stop feeling like a disaster survivor and start feeling like herself again, but she could not imagine how silence would ever feel safe—or how she could ever look Mr. Parker in the eye again without falling apart.
